Proportionality in Administrative Penalties: From Wednesbury to Structured Proportionality

The traditional Wednesbury test asks whether a decision is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have reached it. In Om Kumar v. Union of India (2000) the Supreme Court imported a structured proportionality analysis for disciplinary penalties: (i) the penalty must pursue a legitimate aim (maintaining discipline, deterrence); (ii) the measure must be suitable to achieve that aim; (iii) it must be necessary — no less severe penalty would suffice; (iv) a fair balance must be struck between the severity of the penalty and the gravity of the misconduct. This four‑step test has been reiterated in State of Punjab v. Ram Singh (2004) and Union of India v. K. S. Subramanian (2015).

Illustratively, dismissal for a single instance of minor negligence (e.g., a clerical error causing a delay of two days) fails the necessity and balancing limbs, whereas dismissal for proven corruption involving public funds satisfies all four limbs. The Court in Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation v. Union of India (2018) held that a penalty of compulsory retirement imposed without an inquiry report violated the necessity limb because a lesser penalty (censure, reduction in rank) was available.

Administrative tribunals and departmental inquiry officers must therefore: (1) record the specific misconduct; (2) cite the relevant conduct rules; (3) evaluate the employee’s past record; (4) consider mitigating circumstances; (5) articulate why a lesser penalty would be inadequate. A penalty order that omits any of these steps is vulnerable to judicial review on proportionality grounds.

Administrative Discretion in Data Governance: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDP Act), 2023 establishes a comprehensive framework for processing digital personal data in India. Section 4 mandates that a Data Fiduciary obtain free, informed, specific, and unambiguous consent before processing, unless an exemption under Section 7 applies (e.g., sovereignty, security, public order). The Act creates the Data Protection Board of India (DPBI) under Section 18, empowered to adjudicate complaints, impose penalties up to ₹250 crore, and issue directions for compliance.

Administrative discretion arises at several junctures: (i) the Central Government may notify “significant data fiduciaries” under Section 10, triggering enhanced obligations (Data Protection Officer, Data Protection Impact Assessment, audit); (ii) the Government may prescribe “legitimate uses” under Section 7(2) where consent is not required, such as for employment records or legal obligations; (iii) the DPBI may issue codes of practice under Section 40, guiding sector‑specific compliance. Each discretionary power is subject to the rule‑making procedure under Section 40(2) — draft rules must be placed before Parliament for thirty days.

The Supreme Court’s Justice K. S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) judgment recognised privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21, anchoring the DPDP Act’s constitutional legitimacy. In WhatsApp LLC v. Union of India (2021) the Court emphasised that any executive action affecting data processing must satisfy the proportionality test — legitimate aim, suitability, necessity, and balancing. Consequently, a decision‑maker invoking a Section 7 exemption must document the specific public‑interest objective, demonstrate that consent‑based processing is impracticable, and show that the exemption is narrowly tailored.

Operational checklist for a Data Fiduciary: (1) map all data flows and classify personal data; (2) implement a consent management platform compliant with Section 4; (3) conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment for high‑risk processing; (4) appoint a Data Protection Officer if notified as significant; (5) establish a grievance redressal mechanism with a 30‑day resolution timeline; (6) maintain records of all exemptions invoked under Section 7 with reasoned orders. Non‑compliance attracts DPBI penalties and possible criminal liability under Section 44.

Administrative Discretion in Fiscal Federalism: Finance Commission Recommendations and Conditional Grants

Article 280 mandates the constitution of a Finance Commission every five years to recommend the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (vertical devolution) and the allocation among States (horizontal devolution). The Fifteenth Finance Commission (2020‑2025) adopted criteria — population (15 %), area (15 %), forest and ecology (10 %), income distance (45 %), demographic performance (12.5 %), and tax effort (2.5 %). Its recommendations are advisory; the President accepts them by order, but the Union Government retains discretion in implementing conditional grants under Articles 275 (grants for welfare of Scheduled Tribes) and 282 (grants for any public purpose).

The Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977) held that Finance Commission recommendations are not justiciable, yet the Union’s discretion to deviate must not be arbitrary. In Bihar v. Union of India (2022) the Court reiterated that conditional grants must satisfy the Article 14 test — the classification of beneficiary States must rest on an intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the grant’s objective. The Centre’s power to attach conditions (e.g., reform milestones, expenditure tracking) is subject to the proportionality principle: conditions must be necessary for achieving the grant’s purpose and not excessively intrude on State autonomy.

Practical guidance for a State Finance Department: (1) analyse the Finance Commission’s devolution formula and identify the State’s entitlement; (2) prepare a compliance matrix for each conditional grant — linking conditions to measurable outputs; (3) negotiate conditionality that respects the State’s legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule; (4) maintain a grant‑utilisation dashboard for real‑time reporting to the Union; (5) seek judicial review only where conditions are manifestly arbitrary or violate the federal balance. This structured approach converts discretionary fiscal transfers into accountable, outcome‑oriented instruments.

  • Assuming that an ESMA notification is immune from judicial review because it concerns essential services; the Supreme Court has repeatedly required a speaking order and material evidence.
  • Treating the Article 14 intelligible differentia test as a mere formality; the rational nexus must be demonstrably linked to the statutory objective.
  • Applying the Wednesbury test alone to disciplinary penalties without the four‑step proportionality analysis mandated since Om Kumar (2000).
  • Believing that the DPDP Act’s Section 7 exemptions can be invoked without a reasoned order; the proportionality requirement from Puttaswamy applies.
  • Assuming Finance Commission recommendations are binding and non‑reviewable; the Union’s implementation discretion is subject to Article 14 and proportionality.
  • Overlooking the mandatory parliamentary laying of delegated legislation under the DPDP Act; absence of laying renders rules procedurally defective.
  • Remember to map the statutory source before invoking constitutional limits.

Administrative Discretion under the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897: Legal Framework, Judicial Review, and Proportionality in Public Health Emergencies

The Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 (EDA) remains the principal statutory instrument empowering the Union and State governments to take extraordinary measures during outbreaks. Section 2 authorises the State Government to prescribe temporary regulations for the inspection, segregation, and treatment of persons suspected of being infected, while Section 2A (inserted by the 2020 amendment) extends similar powers to the Central Government for inter‑state matters. Section 3 penalises disobedience with imprisonment up to six months or fine, and Section 4 provides immunity for actions taken in good faith under the Act. The breadth of the delegation is deliberately wide: the executive may restrict movement, close markets, mandate vaccination, or requisition private property without prior legislative sanction.

Judicial review of EDA orders follows the constitutional template of Article 14 and Article 21. The Supreme Court in K. S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) established the four‑step proportionality test — legitimate aim, suitability, necessity, and balancing — which has been applied to lockdown notifications, quarantine orders, and compulsory testing directives. In WhatsApp LLC v. Union of India (2021) the Court reiterated that any executive action affecting fundamental rights must be supported by a speaking order that records the factual basis, the statutory provision invoked, and the proportionality reasoning. High Courts have consistently set aside orders that lack a reasoned justification, treating the absence of a speaking order as a violation of the principle of natural justice and the non‑arbitrariness requirement under Article 14.

Operationally, a decision‑maker invoking the EDA should: (1) identify the specific statutory provision (Section 2 or 2A) and the precise public‑health objective; (2) gather epidemiological data — case positivity rate, reproduction number, hospital capacity — to demonstrate suitability; (3) assess whether less restrictive alternatives (targeted containment, advisories) would achieve the same aim, satisfying the necessity limb; (4) document the balancing exercise, weighing the restriction on livelihood, movement, and privacy against the projected reduction in transmission; (5) issue a written order with a clear expiry date and a review mechanism. Failure to adhere to this checklist exposes the order to judicial invalidation and may attract departmental proceedings for abuse of discretion.

Regulatory Impact Assessment in Delegated Legislation: Cost‑Benefit Analysis, Stakeholder Consultation, and Post‑Implementation Review

Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) has become an established framework for ensuring that subordinate legislation — rules, regulations, notifications — meets the standards of rationality, transparency, and proportionality. The Cabinet Secretariat’s 2017 Guidelines for Regulatory Impact Assessment require every ministry to prepare an RIA statement before finalising any rule that imposes significant compliance costs, alters market structure, or affects fundamental rights. The statement must contain: (a) a clear problem definition; (b) a range of policy options including the status‑quo; (c) quantitative and qualitative cost‑benefit analysis using discounted cash‑flow techniques where feasible; (d) a stakeholder consultation log with summaries of comments received and the ministry’s response; and (e) a monitoring and evaluation plan with measurable indicators for post‑implementation review after twelve to twenty‑four months.

The General Financial Rules, 2017 (as amended in 2022) embed RIA into the rule‑making workflow by mandating that any draft rule with a financial implication exceeding ₹10 crore be accompanied by an RIA note vetted by the Ministry of Finance. The Supreme Court in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) held that delegated legislation must satisfy the test of reasonableness under Article 14, and the subsequent jurisprudence in K. S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) imported the proportionality framework into the scrutiny of executive rule‑making. Consequently, a rule that fails to demonstrate that its benefits outweigh its costs, or that omits meaningful consultation, is vulnerable to being struck down as arbitrary.

From a practitioner’s perspective, the RIA workflow proceeds in five stages: (1) Screening — determine whether the proposed rule crosses the materiality threshold; (2) Scoping — define the analytical boundary, identify affected groups, and select the analytical tools (cost‑effectiveness, cost‑utility, multi‑criteria analysis); (3) Analysis — populate the cost‑benefit matrix, conduct sensitivity analysis, and draft the consultation paper; (4) Consultation — publish the draft rule and RIA summary on the ministry’s website and the Unified Portal for a minimum of thirty days, hold public hearings where required; (5) Decision and Publication — incorporate feedback, finalise the RIA statement, obtain ministerial approval, and lay the rule before Parliament under the relevant statutory laying provision. Post‑implementation, the ministry must submit a review report to the Cabinet Secretariat, which may recommend amendment, repeal, or continuation.

Technique: Proportionality‑Based RIA Checklist
A Ministry proposes a notification under the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 mandating compulsory vaccination for all adults in a district with a 12 % positivity rate. The notification is issued without an RIA, without a speaking order, and without a sunset clause. Identify the three most critical legal deficiencies and the constitutional provisions they violate.
1. Absence of a speaking order — violates the requirement of reasoned decision‑making under Article 14 (non‑arbitrariness) and the principle of natural justice; the Supreme Court in WhatsApp LLC v. Union of India (2021) mandates that any executive action curtailing fundamental rights must record the factual basis and proportionality reasoning. 2. Failure to conduct a Regulatory Impact Assessment — breaches the Cabinet Secretariat’s 2017 RIA Guidelines and the General Financial Rules, 2022 amendment, which require cost‑benefit analysis and stakeholder consultation for rules with significant compliance impact; omission renders the rule procedurally ultra vires. 3. Lack of a sunset clause and review mechanism — contravenes the proportionality limb of necessity and balancing (Article 21 read with Article 14) as established in K. S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017); an open‑ended restriction without periodic review is presumptively disproportionate.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question presents an administrative order under a special statute (EDA, Disaster Management Act, Essential Services Maintenance Act), first locate the statutory source of power, then run the four‑step proportionality test mentally. If the order lacks a speaking order, an RIA, or a sunset clause, mark it as vulnerable to judicial review under Articles 14 and 21. This two‑layer filter — statutory competence + constitutional proportionality — solves most situational‑judgment items on administrative discretion.

Decision‑Making in Electoral Administration: Powers of the Election Commission, Model Code of Conduct, and Judicial Oversight

Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction, and control of elections in the Election Commission of India (ECI), a constitutional body insulated from executive interference. The ECI’s decision‑making spans three domains: (a) electoral roll management — inclusion, deletion, and correction of entries under the Representation of the People Act, 1950; (b) poll conduct — notification of election schedules, deployment of observers, and enforcement of the Model Code of Conduct (MCC); and (c) dispute resolution — adjudication of election petitions under the Representation of the People Act, 1951, and disqualification matters under Article 102/191.

The MCC, though not statutorily enacted, acquires constitutional force through the ECI’s plenary power under Article 324. The Supreme Court in Election Commission of India v. State of Tamil Nadu (1993) held that the MCC is enforceable as a directive flowing from the Commission’s constitutional mandate, and any violation attracts the Commission’s power to issue directions, censure, or recommend prosecution. In Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms (2002) the Court mandated disclosure of criminal antecedents, assets, and educational qualifications, expanding the informational basis for voter decision‑making. The Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013) judgment struck down Section 8(4) of the 1951 Act, making disqualification upon conviction immediate, thereby sharpening the ECI’s role in certifying candidate eligibility.

Judicial oversight operates through two channels: (1) Article 32/226 writ jurisdiction — the Supreme Court and High Courts entertain petitions challenging ECI orders on grounds of arbitrariness, mala fides, or violation of fundamental rights; (2) Election petition jurisdiction — High Courts hear petitions under Section 80‑81 of the 1951 Act, reviewing procedural irregularities, corrupt practices, and MCC breaches. The Court in Public Interest Foundation v. Union of India (2019) directed the ECI to publish candidate affidavits within 48 hours, reinforcing transparency. Decision‑makers within the ECI therefore follow a structured protocol: (i) verify statutory competence; (ii) apply the MCC consistently across parties; (iii) record reasons for any coercive direction; (iv) ensure compliance with Supreme Court timelines for affidavit publication and criminal‑case disclosure.

Decision‑Making in Financial Administration: Public Financial Management System, Direct Benefit Transfer, and Outcome‑Based Budgeting

The Public Financial Management System (PFMS), launched in 2009, provides a unified electronic platform for tracking fund flow from the Consolidated Fund of India to implementing agencies down to the last beneficiary. PFMS integrates with the Core Banking Solution of the Reserve Bank of India, enabling real‑time reconciliation of releases, expenditures, and unspent balances. The Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) programme, inaugurated on 1 January 2013, leverages PFMS and Aadhaar‑based authentication to route subsidies — LPG, fertiliser, scholarships, pensions — directly into beneficiaries’ bank accounts, eliminating intermediaries and reducing leakages estimated at a significant proportion in pre‑DBT regimes.

Outcome‑based budgeting, mandated from the 2005‑06 Union Budget, requires each ministry to link financial outlays to measurable outputs and outcomes through a Performance Budget and an Outcome Budget. The Fifteenth Finance Commission (2020‑25) reinforced this approach by recommending that a portion of vertical devolution be conditional on States achieving defined output indicators in health, education, and agriculture. A 2021 Comptroller and Auditor General performance audit on DBT highlighted that while Aadhaar seeding improved targeting, exclusion errors persisted in remote regions, prompting the Ministry of Finance to issue a subsequent circular mandating a grievance‑redressal module within PFMS for beneficiary‑level complaints.

For a financial decision‑maker, the operational checklist is: (1) map the scheme’s fund flow on PFMS and verify that all implementing agencies are onboarded; (2) ensure Aadhaar‑based authentication is compliant with the Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016 and the Supreme Court’s K. S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) judgment on privacy and proportionality; (3) link budget outlays to output‑outcome frameworks in the Performance and Outcome Budgets; (4) institute periodic reconciliation and social‑audit mechanisms to detect exclusion errors.

Administrative Discretion in Public Health Insurance: The Ayushman Bharat Scheme and the National Health Authority

The Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB‑PMJAY), launched on 23 September 2018, is among the world’s largest publicly funded health‑insurance programmes, targeting over 10 crore vulnerable families. The National Health Authority (NHA), constituted by a Gazette notification in 2019, exercises wide‑ranging discretion in (i) defining the benefit package and package rates, (ii) empanelling public and private hospitals, (iii) setting eligibility verification protocols, and (iv) designing the IT platform (the Beneficiary Identification System and the Transaction Management System). The NHA’s discretion is bounded by the statutory framework: the Scheme’s guidelines, the National Health Policy 2017, and the Supreme Court’s jurisprudence on the right to health under Article 21 (e.g., Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity v. State of West Bengal, 1996). The NHA must also comply with the Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016, and the K. S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) proportionality test when linking beneficiary data to Aadhaar.

Key discretionary levers include the annual revision of Health Benefit Packages (HBPs) based on cost‑effectiveness analysis, the power to suspend or de‑empanel hospitals for fraud or quality lapses, and the authority to approve state‑specific top‑up packages. The NHA’s decision‑making follows a structured protocol: (1) evidence‑based clinical‑economic evaluation by the Health Technology Assessment Unit; (2) stakeholder consultation with state health agencies, insurance companies, and provider associations; (3) publication of draft revisions for public comment (minimum 30 days); (4) final notification with reasoned order. Judicial review of NHA orders is available under Article 226/32 on grounds of arbitrariness, mala fides, or violation of fundamental rights. Courts have upheld de‑empanelment orders where the authority recorded reasons and afforded a hearing, illustrating the procedural safeguards that constrain discretion.

For the aspirant, the operational checklist when analysing an NHA decision is: (a) identify the statutory source of the power (NHA notification, Scheme guidelines); (b) verify that the decision follows the prescribed consultation and publication steps; (c) assess whether the proportionality test (legitimate aim, suitability, necessity, balancing) is satisfied, especially when privacy‑impacting data linkages are involved; (d) check for any conflict‑of‑interest safeguards (e.g., independent appraisal committees).

Administrative Discretion in Urban Governance: The Smart Cities Mission and Municipal Decision‑Making

The Smart Cities Mission (SCM), launched on 25 June 2015, selects 100 cities through a competitive challenge process and allocates central assistance of ₹48,000 crore over five years. Each selected city establishes a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) — a corporate entity under the Companies Act, 2013 — which exercises delegated discretion in project identification, procurement, and implementation. The SPV’s board comprises the municipal commissioner (chair), representatives of the state government, and independent directors, thereby blending administrative and corporate governance. Discretionary powers include: (i) prioritising projects under the “Area‑Based Development” and “Pan‑City” components; (ii) selecting technology partners through transparent e‑tendering; (iii) re‑allocating funds across components within the approved Smart City Proposal (SCP); and (iv) setting performance benchmarks for service‑level agreements.

The legal basis for SPV discretion derives from the Mission Guidelines (2015, revised 2020), the respective state municipal acts, and the 74th Constitutional Amendment (Article 243W) which empowers municipalities to perform functions listed in the Twelfth Schedule. However, the SPV’s decisions are subject to (a) the General Financial Rules (GFR) 2017 for procurement; (b) the Right to Information Act, 2005 for transparency; (c) the Comptroller and Auditor General’s audit mandate; and (d) judicial review under Article 226 for arbitrariness or violation of statutory procedure. High Courts have quashed SPV contract awards where evaluation criteria were altered post‑tender without recording reasons, underscoring the duty to give reasoned decisions.

A decision‑maker in an SPV must therefore follow a procedural matrix: (1) confirm that the project aligns with the approved SCP and the city’s Comprehensive Mobility Plan; (2) conduct a Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) for major capital works; (3) publish tender documents on the Government e‑Marketplace (GeM) and allow a minimum 21‑day bidding window; (4) record minutes of the technical and financial evaluation committees with dissent notes; (5) obtain board approval with a resolution that references the statutory authority and the proportionality rationale. The Mission’s outcome‑based monitoring framework (the “Smart Cities Dashboard”) further constrains discretion by linking fund releases to verified physical and financial milestones.

Technique: Applying the Proportionality Test to Discretionary Health Coverage Decisions
A state health authority proposes to exclude a high‑cost oncology drug from the Ayushman Bharat benefit package on the ground that the drug’s incremental cost‑effectiveness ratio (ICER) exceeds the threshold of ₹5 lakh per QALY. The drug manufacturer challenges the exclusion, arguing that the decision violates the right to health under Article 21 and the principle of non‑discrimination. How should a court evaluate the authority’s decision?
Step 1 – Identify the statutory source. The NHA notification and Scheme guidelines empower the NHA to revise HBPs based on clinical‑economic evidence. Step 2 – Verify procedural compliance. Check whether the Health Technology Assessment Unit conducted an ICER analysis, whether the draft revision was published for public comment (≥30 days), and whether the final order records reasons. Step 3 – Apply the four‑limb proportionality test. (a) Legitimate aim: ensuring financial sustainability of the scheme. (b) Suitability: the ICER threshold is a rational method to allocate limited resources. (c) Necessity: no less restrictive alternative (e.g., risk‑sharing agreements) was considered — if the authority ignored such options, the measure fails necessity. (d) Balancing: weigh the health impact on the affected patient cohort against the budgetary impact on the scheme. Step 4 – Judicial review standard. Courts will not substitute their own ICER judgment but will intervene if the decision is arbitrary, mala fide, or procedurally flawed. Conclusion: If the authority followed the prescribed process, considered alternatives, and recorded a reasoned balancing, the exclusion withstands proportionality scrutiny; otherwise, it is liable to be set aside.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks you to evaluate an administrative discretion, first locate the enabling statute or guideline, then run the proportionality checklist (aim, suitability, necessity, balancing). In time‑pressed MCQs, eliminate options that ignore procedural safeguards (public consultation, reasoned order) or that treat discretion as unfettered. Remember that the Supreme Court’s “Wednesbury unreasonableness” test has been largely supplanted by structured proportionality in health‑policy and urban‑governance contexts.

Administrative Discretion in Labour Regulation: The Code on Wages, 2019 and the Role of the Chief Labour Commissioner

The Code on Wages, 2019 consolidates four erstwhile statutes — the Payment of Wages Act, 1936; the Minimum Wages Act, 1948; the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965; and the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 — into a single framework. The Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) (CLC), appointed under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, exercises quasi‑judicial and administrative discretion in (i) adjudicating claims for unpaid wages, overtime, and bonus; (ii) issuing directions for compliance with minimum‑wage notifications; (iii) approving exemptions for certain establishments under the relevant Code provisions; and (iv) monitoring the implementation of the floor‑wage mechanism introduced by the Code. The CLC’s orders are appealable to the Labour Appellate Tribunal and, thereafter, to the High Court under Article 226.

Discretionary boundaries are set by: (a) the Code’s mandatory provisions — e.g., the floor wage cannot be undercut by state notifications; (b) the principle of “equal pay for equal work” (Article 39(d) read with the Equal Remuneration Act); (c) the Supreme Court’s ruling in Air India Statutory Corporation v. United Labour Union (1997) that administrative discretion in labour matters must be exercised fairly and transparently; and (d) the requirement under the Code to record reasons for any exemption or direction. High Courts have set aside exemptions where the CLC failed to consult the tripartite committee and did not record the economic justification, illustrating the procedural rigour expected.

For a decision‑maker, the compliance matrix is: (1) verify that the minimum‑wage notification for the relevant scheduled employment is in force; (2) ensure that any exemption application is accompanied by a financial viability report and a tripartite recommendation; (3) conduct a hearing with the employer and employee representatives before passing an order; (4) issue a speaking order referencing the specific Code sections, the floor‑wage benchmark, and the proportionality rationale; (5) upload the order on the Shram Suvidha Portal within 48 hours for transparency.

Administrative Discretion in Competition Law Enforcement: The Competition Commission of India’s Investigative and Adjudicatory Powers

The Competition Commission of India (CCI), established under the Competition Act, 2002 (as amended in 2007 and 2023), wields broad discretion in (i) initiating inquiries suo motu or on reference; (ii) directing the Director General (DG) to investigate alleged anti‑competitive agreements, abuse of dominance, and combinations; (iii) passing interim orders under Section 33 to prevent irreparable harm; and (iv) imposing penalties up to 10 % of average turnover for the preceding three financial years. The 2023 amendment introduced a “settlement and commitment” framework, expanding the CCI’s discretionary toolkit to resolve cases without full adjudication.

Judicial review of CCI orders follows a two‑tier structure: (a) the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) hears appeals on merits; (b) the Supreme Court entertains statutory appeals under Section 53T and constitutional writs under Article 136. The Supreme Court in Competition Commission of India v. Steel Authority of India Ltd. (2010) held that the CCI’s investigative discretion is subject to the “reasonable suspicion” standard — the Commission must record prima facie reasons before directing a DG investigation. In Google LLC v. Competition Commission of India (2022), the NCLAT upheld a penalty for abuse of dominance in the Android ecosystem, affirming that the CCI’s market‑definition discretion is reviewable only for manifest error.

A competition‑law decision‑maker must therefore: (1) document the prima facie case with specific market‑definition analysis and evidence of appreciable adverse effect on competition (AAEC); (2) ensure the DG’s investigation respects the principles of natural justice (right to be heard, access to non‑confidential evidence); (3) apply the “effects‑based” test for abuse of dominance post‑2023 amendment, moving away from per se rules; (4) when invoking interim orders, satisfy the triple test of prima facie case, balance of convenience, and irreparable injury; (5) record detailed reasons for any settlement or commitment acceptance, including the public‑interest justification.

  • Confusing the NHA’s policy‑making discretion with the state health department’s implementation discretion — they operate under different statutory sources.
  • Assuming SPVs under the Smart Cities Mission are exempt from GFR procurement rules because they are corporate entities.
  • Treating the Chief Labour Commissioner’s exemption power as unfettered, ignoring the mandatory tripartite consultation and floor‑wage floor.
  • Overlooking the “reasonable suspicion” threshold for CCI’s DG investigation direction, leading to an answer that the Commission can investigate at will.
  • Neglecting the proportionality balancing step when a health‑coverage exclusion is challenged on Article 21 grounds.
  • Failing to distinguish between the CCI’s adjudicatory penalty power (up to 10 % turnover) and the settlement framework’s voluntary commitments.
  • Remember that every discretionary order must be a speaking order referencing the enabling provision, the factual matrix, and the proportionality rationale.

Administrative Discretion in the Implementation of the National Education Policy 2020

The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 replaces the 1986 policy and grants the Ministry of Education, state education departments, and autonomous bodies such as the National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) and the University Grants Commission (UGC) wide discretionary powers to translate policy goals into regulatory frameworks. The policy’s “light but tight” regulatory philosophy means that while the central government sets broad standards — curricular framework, teacher‑education norms, accreditation benchmarks — the actual rule‑making, funding allocation, and monitoring are delegated to state governments and institutional heads. This delegation is codified through the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act amendments, the proposed Higher Education Commission of India (HECI) Bill, and the National Curriculum Framework (NCF) revision process.

Key discretionary nodes include: (1) the determination of “equitable quality” thresholds for school infrastructure under Section 19 of the RTE Act, where state governments may notify additional norms beyond the central minimum; (2) the design of the four‑year undergraduate programme with multiple entry‑exit options, where universities exercise autonomy to structure credit‑transfer mechanisms subject to UGC’s Credit Framework for Undergraduate Programmes; (3) the accreditation of teacher‑education institutions by the National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE), where the Council may grant conditional recognition based on infrastructure audits; and (4) the allocation of the “Gender Inclusion Fund” and “Special Education Zones” where district‑level committees decide eligibility criteria.

Judicial scrutiny of these discretionary decisions follows the Wednesbury unreasonableness test refined by the proportionality doctrine in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and University of Delhi v. Rajesh Kumar (2021). Courts have struck down state notifications that imposed teacher‑pupil ratios stricter than the RTE baseline without a reasoned justification, holding that such excesses violate Article 14’s non‑arbitrariness requirement. Conversely, the Supreme Court upheld the UGC’s 2022 directive mandating a minimum 75 % attendance for online degrees, finding the rule proportionate to the policy objective of academic rigour.

For a decision‑maker, the compliance matrix is: (a) verify that any state‑level rule derives its authority from a specific enabling provision in the RTE Act, the UGC Act, or the forthcoming HECI Act; (b) conduct a stakeholder consultation with School Management Committees, parent‑teacher associations, and faculty senates, recording minutes; (c) prepare a speaking order that cites the policy objective, the statutory source, the factual basis (e.g., infrastructure audit report), and the proportionality analysis; (d) publish the order on the state education portal and the National Scholarship Portal within 30 days for transparency.

Decision‑Making under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code: The Role of the National Company Law Tribunal and the Insolvency Professional

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016, creates a time‑bound, creditor‑driven resolution framework where the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and the Insolvency Professional (IP) exercise layered discretion. The NCLT’s discretionary powers arise at three critical junctures: (i) admission of a corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) under Section 7 (financial creditor), Section 9 (operational creditor), or Section 10 (corporate applicant); (ii) approval or rejection of a resolution plan under Section 31, where the Tribunal must satisfy itself that the plan meets the “feasibility and viability” test and complies with the “fair and equitable” distribution mandated by Section 30(2); and (iii) ordering liquidation under Section 33 when no plan is approved or the approved plan fails.

The IP, appointed by the Committee of Creditors (CoC), wields discretion in (a) managing the corporate debtor’s affairs as a going concern, including the power to raise interim finance under Section 25(2); (b) verifying and admitting claims, where the IP may reject a claim for lack of documentary proof, subject to appeal to the NCLT; and (c) preparing the information memorandum and inviting resolution plans, where the IP sets eligibility criteria such as net‑worth thresholds and sectoral experience, provided they are non‑discriminatory and disclosed in the request for resolution plans.

Landmark judgments shape the boundaries of this discretion. In Essar Steel India Ltd. v. Satish Kumar Gupta (2019), the Supreme Court held that the CoC’s commercial wisdom is paramount but not immune from judicial review for “manifest arbitrariness”. The Court also clarified that the NCLT cannot modify the distribution mechanism prescribed in Section 53, limiting its discretion to procedural compliance. In K. Sashidhar v. Indian Overseas Bank (2019), the Court ruled that the NCLT may not reject a resolution plan solely because a dissenting financial creditor prefers liquidation, reinforcing the primacy of the CoC’s majority vote (66 % voting share). The 2020 amendment introduced Section 29A disqualifications, expanding the IP’s duty to screen applicants for eligibility, a discretionary filter that has been upheld as a legitimate legislative objective.

A decision‑maker’s checklist: (1) confirm that the admission application contains a default of at least ₹1 crore and a record of the debt; (2) ensure the IP publishes the public announcement within three days of appointment and constitutes the CoC within 30 days; (3) verify that the resolution plan includes a payment schedule for operational creditors not less than the liquidation value, as mandated by Section 30(2)(b); (4) record detailed reasons for any rejection of a plan, referencing the specific statutory criteria; (5) upload the order on the NCLT e‑filing portal and the IBBI website within 48 hours.

Worked Scenario
A financial creditor files a Section 7 application against a corporate debtor. The debtor contests, arguing that the debt is disputed because an arbitration award is pending. The NCLT admits the application. The debtor appeals, claiming the Tribunal erred in exercising discretion without determining the existence of a “dispute” under Section 7(5). How should the appellate authority decide?
Under Section 7(5) of the IBC, the NCLT must reject the application if a “dispute” exists — defined as a bona fide disagreement on the existence or amount of the debt, not merely a pending arbitration. In M/s. Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank (2018), the Supreme Court held that a dispute must be “real and substantial”, not frivolous. Since the arbitration award is pending but the debt is acknowledged in the contract and the creditor has a decree‑worthy claim, the NCLT’s admission is justified. The appellate authority should uphold the admission, noting that the Tribunal recorded reasons that the arbitration does not extinguish the debt and that the creditor’s claim meets the ₹1 crore threshold. The decision‑maker must ensure the order references Section 7(5), the Innoventive precedent, and the factual finding that the dispute is not bona fide.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks you to choose the correct sequence of discretionary steps under the IBC, map each step to its statutory section: admission (Sec 7/9/10) → CoC constitution (Sec 21) → IP’s claim verification (Sec 14) → resolution plan invitation (Sec 25) → CoC approval (Sec 30) → NCLT sanction (Sec 31). Any answer that places CoC approval before claim verification or NCLT sanction before CoC vote is automatically wrong. Memorise the 180‑day CIRP timeline (extendable by 90 days) and the 66 % voting threshold; these numbers appear in at least two MCQs every year.

Administrative Discretion in the Regulation of Emerging Technologies: Drones, Artificial Intelligence, and Blockchain

The rapid proliferation of drones, artificial intelligence (AI) systems, and blockchain‑based applications has compelled the Ministry of Civil Aviation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to issue sector‑specific regulatory frameworks that confer substantial discretion on designated authorities. The Drone Rules, 2021 (notified under the Aircraft Act, 1934) empower the Director General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) to classify airspace into green, yellow, and red zones, to grant or deny Unique Identification Numbers (UIN) and Unmanned Aircraft Operator Permits (UAOP), and to impose operational conditions such as beyond‑visual‑line‑of‑sight (BVLOS) approvals. The DGCA’s discretion is bounded by the “risk‑based” approach: green‑zone operations require only a self‑declaration, while yellow‑zone and red‑zone flights need prior permission, with the DGCA required to record reasons for any denial.

In the AI domain, MeitY’s “National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence” (2023) and the forthcoming Digital India Act propose a regulatory sandbox where the Ministry may grant “experimental licences” to start‑ups for testing high‑risk AI models (e.g., facial‑recognition, autonomous decision‑making). The sandbox authority exercises discretion in selecting participants based on criteria such as data‑governance maturity, societal impact assessment, and compliance with the proposed “Algorithmic Transparency” standards. Judicial review of sandbox decisions will likely invoke the proportionality test from K. S. Puttaswamy and the non‑arbitrariness principle under Article 14, requiring the authority to demonstrate that the selection criteria are objective, published, and applied uniformly.

Blockchain regulation currently rests on the RBI’s 2018 circular (later set aside by the Supreme Court in Internet and Mobile Association of India v. RBI, 2020) and the 2023 “Virtual Digital Assets” taxation framework under the Finance Act. The RBI retains discretion to issue “guidelines” for entities dealing in crypto‑assets, including Know‑Your‑Customer (KYC) norms, transaction‑monitoring thresholds, and reporting obligations to the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU). The 2023 amendment to the Prevention of Money‑Laundering Act (PMLA) brings virtual digital asset service providers within the definition of “reporting entities”, expanding the Director, FIU’s discretion to demand records and impose penalties for non‑compliance.

For a decision‑maker, the compliance matrix across the three technologies is: (1) verify that any drone‑zone classification order cites the specific rule (Rule 12 of Drone Rules) and includes a risk‑assessment report; (2) ensure AI sandbox selection orders reference the published eligibility matrix, the applicant’s impact‑assessment dossier, and a proportionality rationale for any exclusion; (3) confirm that crypto‑asset directives are issued under the PMLA’s Section 12(1)(a) and that the reporting entity has been given a hearing before any penalty is imposed. All orders must be uploaded on the respective portal (Digital Sky, MeitY sandbox portal, FIU‑India) within the statutory time‑frames.

Decision‑Making in Preventive Detention: The National Security Act, 1980 and Judicial Safeguards

The National Security Act (NSA), 1980, empowers the Central Government and State Governments to detain a person without trial for up to twelve months (extendable to twenty‑four months in certain cases) to prevent them from acting in a manner prejudicial to the security of the State, the maintenance of public order, or the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community. The Act creates a two‑tier discretionary structure: (i) the detaining authority (District Magistrate or Commissioner of Police) issues the detention order under Section 3; (ii) the Advisory Board, constituted under Section 9 and chaired by a High Court judge, reviews the order within three weeks and recommends confirmation, modification, or revocation.

The Supreme Court in A. K. Roy v. Union of India (1982) upheld the constitutional validity of the NSA but imposed strict procedural safeguards: the detaining authority must record “subjective satisfaction” based on “relevant material”, the grounds of detention must be communicated to the detenu in a language they understand, and the detenu must be afforded the earliest opportunity to make a representation against the order. In K. A. N. S. v. State of Tamil Nadu (2020), the Court held that the Advisory Board’s recommendation is not binding on the government, but the government must record reasons if it disagrees, thereby introducing a quasi‑judicial review layer.

Recent amendments (2021) introduced a mandatory “periodic review” every six months by a Review Committee headed by the Chief Secretary, adding a further discretionary checkpoint. The Committee may order release if it finds the detention no longer necessary, but its decision is subject to judicial review under Article 226 for Wednesbury unreasonableness. The Court in Mohd. Rafiq v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2022) emphasized that the “subjective satisfaction” must be based on contemporaneous material, not stale intelligence, and that the detaining authority cannot rely solely on police reports without independent verification.

A decision‑maker’s checklist: (1) ensure the detention order cites the specific clause of Section 3 (security of State, public order, or essential supplies) and attaches the material relied upon; (2) serve the grounds on the detenu within five days, with a translation if required; (3) constitute the Advisory Board within three weeks and provide the detenu a copy of the Board’s report; (4) if the government rejects the Board’s recommendation, issue a speaking order explaining the disagreement; (5) conduct the six‑monthly Review Committee meeting, record minutes, and publish the outcome on the state home department website.

Administrative Discretion in Public Sector Undertaking Disinvestment and Strategic Sale

The Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM) under the Ministry of Finance exercises broad discretion in designing and executing disinvestment transactions — ranging from minority stake sales through Offer for Sale (OFS) on stock exchanges to strategic sales involving transfer of management control. The legal framework derives from the Government Companies (Appointment of Directors) Rules, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018, and the specific Cabinet approvals for each transaction. The discretionary nodes include: (i) selection of the transaction modality (OFS, strategic sale, asset monetisation via InvITs/REITs); (ii) determination of the floor price or reserve price, which must be justified by an independent valuation report from a SEBI‑registered valuer; (iii) setting eligibility criteria for bidders, such as net‑worth, sectoral experience, and “fit and proper” tests; and (iv) deciding on the extent of government shareholding to be retained (e.g., 51 % in strategic sectors like defence, atomic energy).

The Supreme Court in Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2019) (the “Air India” case) held that the government’s disinvestment policy is a “policy decision” amenable to limited judicial review — only for manifest arbitrariness, mala fides, or violation of statutory mandate. The Court mandated that the Cabinet note must record the rationale for the chosen modality, the valuation methodology, and the expected fiscal impact. The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) audits each transaction post‑facto, and its reports have highlighted instances where the floor price was set below the valuer’s lower bound without recorded justification, leading to parliamentary scrutiny.

The 2021 “Strategic Disinvestment Policy” introduced a “Core” and “Non‑Core” classification, granting the NITI Aayog discretion to recommend sectors for strategic sale. The policy also requires a “Competitive Bidding Process” with a minimum of two qualified bidders; if only one bidder qualifies, the transaction may proceed only with a “Swiss Challenge” mechanism, where the original bidder can match a superior offer. The decision‑maker must ensure that the Swiss Challenge terms are pre‑disclosed in the Request for Proposal (RFP) and that the evaluation committee records a comparative analysis of the bids.

Compliance matrix for a disinvestment officer: (1) obtain Cabinet approval with a detailed note covering valuation, modality, and fiscal targets; (2) appoint a Transaction Advisor and a Legal Advisor through a transparent selection process; (3) publish the Preliminary Information Memorandum (PIM) and RFP on the DIPAM website and the stock exchange platform; (4) conduct a pre‑bid conference, record minutes, and issue clarifications; (5) evaluate bids against the pre‑disclosed criteria, prepare a Comparative Evaluation Report, and submit to the Core Group of Secretaries for recommendation; (6) issue a speaking order approving the successful bidder, referencing the valuation report, the evaluation matrix, and the Cabinet approval; (7) complete the share transfer and file the requisite forms with the Registrar of Companies and SEBI within the statutory timelines.

  • Confusing the DGCA’s zone‑classification discretion with the Ministry’s policy‑making power — they derive from different statutory provisions.
  • Assuming the Advisory Board’s recommendation under the NSA is binding on the government; the government may disagree but must record reasons.
  • Treating the NCLT’s power to approve a resolution plan as unfettered; the Tribunal cannot alter the statutory waterfall in Section 53.
  • Overlooking the requirement that a strategic disinvestment floor price be supported by an independent valuer’s report and a Cabinet note.
  • Neglecting the mandatory six‑monthly Review Committee under the NSA, leading to an answer that detention can continue indefinitely without review.
  • Failing to distinguish between the AI sandbox’s experimental licence (discretionary, non‑binding) and a full regulatory approval (binding, subject to legislative enactment).
  • These traps highlight the need for precise statutory referencing in every answer.

Appellate Decision‑Making under the Right to Information Act: The Central Information Commission’s Jurisprudence

The Right to Information Act, 2005 (RTI Act) establishes a two‑tier appellate mechanism. Section 19(1) requires the applicant to file a first appeal before the First Appellate Authority (FAA) within 30 days of the Public Information Officer’s (PIO) decision. If the FAA does not dispose of the appeal within 30 days, or the appellant is aggrieved by the order, a second appeal lies to the Central Information Commission (CIC) under Section 19(3) within 90 days from the date of the FAA’s order. The CIC, constituted under Section 12, comprises a Chief Information Commissioner and up to ten Information Commissioners appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee headed by the Prime Minister. The 2019 amendment (Act 24 of 2019) fixed the tenure of Commissioners at three years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier, and removed the earlier provision linking their status to that of a Supreme Court judge.

The CIC’s powers include the authority to require the public authority to provide information, impose a penalty of up to ₹25,000 on the PIO for mala fide denial, and recommend disciplinary action. Landmark jurisprudence has shaped the scope of these powers. In Central Board of Secondary Education v. Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011) the Supreme Court held that answer‑scripts are “personal information” exempt under Section 8(1)(j) unless larger public interest warrants disclosure. Namit Sharma v. Union of India (2013) clarified that third‑party information can be disclosed only after giving the third party a reasonable opportunity to be heard. The Supreme Court’s decision in Anjali Bhardwaj v. Union of India reinforced the functional independence of the CIC, directing the government to fill vacancies within a stipulated period and to insulate the Commission from executive interference.

Procedurally, the appellant must attach a copy of the FAA’s order, the original RTI application, and an index of documents. The CIC may conduct hearings via video‑conference, a practice adopted during the COVID‑19 pandemic and retained thereafter. The Commission’s orders are binding; non‑compliance can be challenged through a writ petition under Article 226 before the High Court. The CIC also publishes an annual report detailing disposal rates, penalty impositions, and systemic recommendations, which serves as a key reference for policy‑level decision‑making on transparency.

Administrative Discretion in the Implementation of the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act

The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 (MGNREGA) guarantees at least 100 days of wage employment per rural household per financial year. The Act vests primary implementation discretion in the Gram Panchayat, which prepares the annual shelf of works, selects beneficiaries, and maintains muster rolls. The District Programme Coordinator (DPC) consolidates Gram Panchayat plans into a district‑level labour budget, while the State Employment Guarantee Council (SEGC) monitors fund flow and social audit compliance. Wage rates are not set by the Panchayat; they are notified by the Central Government each year based on the Consumer Price Index for Agricultural Labourers (CPI‑AL), ensuring uniformity across states.

Discretionary nodes include: (i) choice of permissible works — water conservation, drought proofing, irrigation canals, and rural connectivity — subject to the “works list” in Schedule I; (ii) determination of the wage‑material ratio (minimum 60:40) for each work; (iii) authorisation of payment through the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) system, which became mandatory from 2017‑18; and (iv) conduct of social audits every six months, facilitated by the Social Audit Unit (SAU) under the State Rural Livelihoods Mission. Subsequent amendments have introduced a “timely payment” clause requiring wage disbursement within 15 days of muster‑roll closure, with interest for delays beyond that period.

Judicial oversight has sharpened the boundaries of this discretion. The Supreme Court has held that persistent wage delays constitute a violation of the fundamental right to livelihood under Article 21 and directed states to institutionalise a real‑time monitoring dashboard. The Court also mandated that the SEGC’s quarterly review meetings be minuted and placed in the public domain. Performance audits by the Comptroller and Auditor General have highlighted deviations from the approved shelf of works, underscoring the need for stricter adherence to the work‑selection protocol.

Technique: Calculating the Second‑Appeal Deadline under the RTI Act
A citizen files an RTI application on 1 January 2024. The PIO replies on 15 January 2024. The citizen files a first appeal on 20 January 2024. The First Appellate Authority disposes of the appeal on 10 February 2024. What is the last date on which the citizen can file a second appeal before the Central Information Commission?
The RTI Act prescribes a 90‑day window from the date of the FAA’s order for the second appeal. Counting 90 days from 10 February 2024 (including the start date) gives 11 May 2024. Therefore, the citizen must file the second appeal on or before 11 May 2024.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the two statutory windows — 30 days for the first appeal and 90 days for the second appeal — and the penalty ceiling of ₹25,000. Use a mental calendar: add three months to the FAA order date and then adjust for the exact day count; this avoids off‑by‑one errors in timed MCQs.

Decision‑Making in the Regulation of Pharmaceuticals: The Central Drugs Standard Control Organization’s Approval Process

The Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, read with the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945, constitutes the primary legislative framework for pharmaceutical regulation in India. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO), headed by the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI), functions as the national regulatory authority under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. The approval pathway for a new drug involves: (i) submission of a Clinical Trial Application (CTA) under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019; (ii) conduct of Phase I‑III trials in accordance with Good Clinical Practice (GCP) guidelines; (iii) filing of a New Drug Application (NDA) containing chemistry, manufacturing, and controls (CMC) data, pre‑clinical and clinical study reports; and (iv) evaluation by the Subject Expert Committee (SEC) followed by DCGI’s marketing authorisation.

During the COVID‑19 pandemic, CDSCO invoked the “Emergency Use Authorisation” (EUA) provision under Rule 122A (inserted in 2020) to grant conditional approvals to vaccines and antivirals. An EUA is distinct from a full marketing authorisation: it is time‑bound, subject to post‑authorisation safety monitoring, and can be revoked if benefit‑risk balance shifts. Amendments to the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules have introduced a mandatory Post‑Marketing Surveillance (PMS) plan for all new approvals, requiring periodic safety update reports (PSURs) at defined intervals.

Judicial pronouncements have clarified the limits of CDSCO’s discretion. The Supreme Court has upheld the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority’s (NPPA) power to fix ceiling prices under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, ruling that pricing decisions are integral to the regulatory regime. The Court also emphasized that CDSCO’s scientific evaluation must be documented through a speaking order, enabling judicial review for arbitrariness under Article 14.

Administrative Discretion in the Allocation of Food Subsidies under the National Food Security Act

The National Food Security Act, 2013 (NFSA) entitles up to 75 % of the rural population and 50 % of the urban population to receive subsidised foodgrains — rice at ₹3/kg, wheat at ₹2/kg, and coarse grains at ₹1/kg — through the Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS). Beneficiary identification is anchored in the Socio‑Economic and Caste Census (SECC) 2011 data, which provides the deprivation criteria (automatic inclusion, automatic exclusion, and scoring). State Food Commissions (SFCs), constituted under Section 16, monitor implementation, hear grievances, and advise the state government on corrective measures.

Key discretionary decisions include: (i) the method of Aadhaar seeding — while the Supreme Court judgment in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) upheld voluntary Aadhaar linkage, many states made it mandatory for ration card portability; (ii) the rollout of the “One Nation One Ration Card” (ONORC) scheme, launched nationally in 2020, which required integration of state PDS databases with the central Integrated Management of Public Distribution System (IM‑PDS) portal; (iii) the operation of Fair Price Shops (FPS) — licensing, viability gap funding, and the introduction of electronic Point‑of‑Sale (e‑PoS) devices for biometric authentication; and (iv) the management of the Food Corporation of India (FCI) stock release calendar, which determines the quantity and timing of grain allocation to states.

The Supreme Court in People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India directed the Centre to address exclusion errors arising from faulty SECC data and to ensure that no eligible household is denied entitlement due to Aadhaar‑related technical failures. Subsequent amendments have institutionalised the ONORC framework, mandating inter‑state portability and real‑time transaction logging. Audit reports by the Comptroller and Auditor General have flagged leakage in grain distribution, prompting the Ministry of Consumer Affairs to issue revised Standard Operating Procedures for FPS monitoring.

Decision‑Making in the Management of Public Grievances: The CPGRAMS Framework and the Department of Administrative Reforms

The Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS) was launched in 2007 and substantially revamped in 2016 to provide a single‑window, IT‑enabled platform for citizens to lodge grievances against central government ministries and departments. The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG), under the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, serves as the nodal agency. CPGRAMS operates on a three‑level escalation matrix: Level 1 — the concerned Ministry/Department (resolution within 30 days); Level 2 — the Department of Administrative Reforms (review within 15 days if Level 1 fails); Level 3 — the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) for unresolved cases of systemic importance.

Each grievance receives a unique registration number, and the citizen can track status via the portal or the “MyGov” mobile app. The 2020 Citizen’s Charter guidelines mandated that every Ministry publish a Grievance Redressal Officer (GRO) directory, define service standards, and display a “Grievance Redressal Timeline” on its website. DARPG has introduced an AI‑based triage module that classifies incoming grievances by urgency, subject matter, and past resolution patterns, auto‑assigning them to the appropriate GRO. The Supreme Court, in a suo‑motu writ, directed all central ministries to ensure that a speaking order is issued at each level, failing which the concerned officer is liable for disciplinary action.

Performance metrics published in recent annual reports indicate a high disposal rate within the prescribed 30‑day window, with an average resolution time of under three weeks. However, reports flag a persistent backlog in the “Pension” and “Taxation” categories, attributing it to inter‑departmental data mismatches. DARPG now requires quarterly audit of grievance data by the Internal Audit Wing and mandatory feedback surveys for complainants, aiming to close the loop between decision‑making and citizen satisfaction.

  • Confusing the 30‑day first‑appeal window with the 90‑day second‑appeal window under the RTI Act.
  • Assuming the Gram Panchayat can unilaterally change the wage rate under MGNREGA; the rate is fixed by the Centre based on CPI‑AL.
  • Treating CDSCO’s emergency use authorisation as a full marketing approval; it is conditional and time‑bound.
  • Overlooking the requirement that NFSA beneficiaries be identified through the SECC 2011 data and not solely by Aadhaar.
  • Believing CPGRAMS resolves grievances automatically; each level must issue a speaking order within the prescribed period.
  • The examiner often mixes the penalty ceiling of ₹25,000 under the RTI Act with penalties under other grievance redressal rules, so always verify the governing statute.

Administrative Discretion in Climate Finance: Green Bonds, Carbon Markets, and the National Adaptation Fund

The Union Ministry of Finance issued India’s first sovereign green bonds in January 2023, raising ₹16,000 crore for projects that meet the Green Bond Framework aligned with the International Capital Market Association’s Green Bond Principles. The framework earmarks proceeds for renewable energy, energy efficiency, pollution prevention, sustainable agriculture, and climate‑resilient infrastructure. Discretion lies with the Department of Economic Affairs (DEA) in selecting eligible projects, verifying additionality, and reporting impact through an annual Green Bond Report audited by the Comptroller and Auditor General. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) acts as the issuing agent and monitors end‑use compliance via a dedicated monitoring cell.

Parallel to sovereign issuance, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) notified the Green Bond Guidelines in 2017, requiring issuers to obtain a second‑party opinion and to disclose the use‑of‑proceeds in the offer document. State‑level entities such as the Tamil Nadu Green Climate Fund and the Kerala Infrastructure Investment Fund Board have leveraged these guidelines to mobilise sub‑national climate finance. The National Adaptation Fund for Climate Change (NAFCC), established under the National Action Plan on Climate Change (2008) and operationalised in 2015, provides grant‑based assistance to states for adaptation projects. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) exercises discretion in approving project proposals, setting co‑financing ratios, and monitoring outcomes through the State Level Steering Committees.

Carbon market mechanisms add another layer of discretion. The Energy Conservation Act, 2001, amended in 2022, empowers the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) to design a domestic carbon credit trading scheme. The Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) cycle, now in its seventh cycle (2023‑24), allocates energy‑saving certificates (ESCerts) to designated consumers; the BEE decides the baseline, the trajectory, and the verification methodology. The upcoming Indian Carbon Market (ICM), envisaged under the 2023 amendment, will allow voluntary trading of Certified Emission Reductions (CERs) and will be governed by a National Carbon Registry administered by the Ministry of Power. Administrative choices on registry architecture, price discovery, and linkage with international mechanisms (e.g., Article 6 of the Paris Agreement) will shape the market’s integrity.

Judicial scrutiny has reinforced procedural rigor. In M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (2021), the Supreme Court directed the Centre to ensure that green bond proceeds are not diverted to non‑green assets, emphasising the doctrine of public trust. The National Green Tribunal (NGT) has also entertained petitions challenging the adequacy of NAFCC disbursements, compelling the MoEFCC to publish quarterly utilisation statements. For aspirants, the key decision‑making nodes are: (i) project selection criteria under the Green Bond Framework; (ii) the PAT baseline‑setting methodology; (iii) the design of the ICM registry; and (iv) the NAFCC appraisal checklist. Each node involves a blend of statutory mandate, executive guideline, and judicial oversight, making them fertile ground for situational‑judgment questions.

Decision‑Making under the National Cyber Security Strategy: Institutional Architecture and Incident Response Protocols

The National Cyber Security Strategy (NCSS) 2020, released by the National Security Council Secretariat (NSCS), outlines a whole‑of‑government approach to protect critical information infrastructure (CII). The strategy identifies three pillars: (1) a robust legal‑policy framework, (2) capacity building and indigenous technology development, and (3) collaborative incident response. The apex decision‑making body is the National Cyber Coordination Centre (NCCC), operational since 2017 under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). The NCCC aggregates threat intelligence from sectoral Computer Emergency Response Teams (CERT‑In for the general internet, CERT‑Fin for banking, CERT‑Power for electricity, etc.) and issues advisories that ministries must implement within prescribed timelines.

Statutory backing comes from the Information Technology Act, 2000 (as amended in 2008) and the Rules thereunder, notably the Information Technology (The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team and Manner of Performing Functions and Duties) Rules, 2013. These rules empower CERT‑In to direct any service provider, intermediary, or body corporate to take specific remedial actions within six hours of a cyber incident notification. The 2022 amendment to the IT Rules introduced a mandatory 72‑hour reporting window for data breaches affecting personal data, aligning with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Non‑compliance attracts penalties up to ₹250 crore under Section 43A of the IT Act.

Sectoral regulators exercise delegated discretion. The Reserve Bank of India’s “Cyber Security Framework for Banks” (2016, updated 2021) mandates a Board‑approved cyber‑risk policy, a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), and quarterly penetration testing. The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) issued similar guidelines for insurers in 2020. The Department of Telecommunications (DoT) enforces the Unified License conditions requiring licensees to maintain a Security Operations Centre (SOC) and to share incident logs with the NCCC. The National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC), designated under the NCIIPC Act, 2014, identifies CII sectors (power, transport, finance, health, etc.) and issues sector‑specific protection guidelines.

Incident response follows a tiered escalation matrix: Level 1 – the affected entity’s internal SOC; Level 2 – sectoral CERT; Level 3 – NCCC; Level 4 – National Crisis Management Committee (NCMC) chaired by the Cabinet Secretary for incidents of national significance. The 2021 ransomware attack on the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) illustrated the matrix: AIIMS’ SOC escalated to CERT‑In, which coordinated with the NCCC and the Ministry of Health; the NCMC was briefed within 24 hours, leading to a whole‑of‑government containment effort. Decision‑making questions often test the aspirant’s ability to identify the correct escalation level, the statutory reporting deadline, and the authority empowered to issue binding directions. The interplay between the IT Act, sectoral regulations, and the NCSS creates a layered discretion space where procedural compliance and substantive proportionality are both examined.

Situational Judgment: Cyber Incident Escalation
A mid‑size power distribution company detects a sophisticated malware intrusion in its SCADA network at 02:15 hrs. The company’s internal SOC isolates the affected segment but cannot eradicate the malware. According to the NCSS and the IT (CERT‑In) Rules, what is the immediate mandatory action the company must take, and within what time frame?
The company must report the incident to CERT‑In (the sectoral CERT for power is CERT‑Power, which operates under CERT‑In) within six hours of detection, as mandated by the Information Technology (The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team and Manner of Performing Functions and Duties) Rules, 2013. Simultaneously, it must inform the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC) because the SCADA system qualifies as Critical Information Infrastructure. The report triggers Level 2 escalation; CERT‑In will coordinate with the NCCC (Level 3) and, if the incident threatens grid stability, the NCMC (Level 4). Failure to report within six hours attracts penal action under Section 43A of the IT Act.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the four‑level escalation matrix (Entity SOC → Sectoral CERT → NCCC → NCMC) and the two statutory reporting windows: six hours for cyber incidents under the CERT‑In Rules and 72 hours for personal‑data breaches under the 2022 IT Rules amendment. When a question describes a sector (banking, power, health), map it to the correct sectoral CERT (CERT‑Fin, CERT‑Power, CERT‑Health) before choosing the answer.

Administrative Discretion in the Regulation of Virtual Digital Assets: The 2023 Bill, Taxation, and Enforcement

The Finance Act, 2023 introduced a comprehensive tax regime for Virtual Digital Assets (VDAs) without enacting a separate legislative framework. Section 115BBH of the Income‑Tax Act, 1961, imposes a flat 30 % tax on income from transfer of VDAs, disallows set‑off of losses against other heads, and permits only the cost of acquisition as deduction. Section 194S mandates a 1 % Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) on consideration exceeding ₹10,000 (₹50,000 for specified persons) per transaction, effective 1 July 2023. The Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) issued Notification No. 13/2023 defining VDAs to include cryptocurrencies, non‑fungible tokens (NFTs), and any other token of similar nature, but explicitly excluding central bank digital currency (CBDC) and loyalty points.

Simultaneously, the Cryptocurrency and Regulation of Official Digital Currency Bill, 2021 (the “Crypto Bill”) lapsed with the dissolution of the 17th Lok Sabha. The government has signalled a consultative approach: the 2023 G20 Presidency produced a “Policy and Regulatory Framework for Crypto‑Assets” that recommends licensing of Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs), AML/KYC obligations aligned with the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) Travel Rule, and a prohibition on unbacked stablecoins. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) continues to enforce its 2018 circular (upheld by the Supreme Court in Internet and Mobile Association of India v. RBI, 2020) prohibiting regulated entities from dealing in VDAs, while the Enforcement Directorate (ED) investigates money‑laundering cases under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, treating VDA transactions as “proceeds of crime” when linked to predicate offences.

Administrative discretion is exercised at multiple levels: (i) the CBDT determines the threshold for TDS applicability and the valuation methodology for cost of acquisition; (ii) the Financial Intelligence Unit‑India (FIU‑IND) issues guidelines for VASP reporting of suspicious transaction reports (STRs); (iii) the Ministry of Finance, through the Department of Economic Affairs, decides on the licensing regime for VASPs once the Crypto Bill is re‑introduced; (iv) the RBI may issue directions under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, to restrict banking channels for unlicensed VASPs. The Supreme Court’s 2020 judgment struck down the RBI’s blanket ban as disproportionate, but left the door open for proportionate regulation. Consequently, any future licensing framework must satisfy the test of reasonableness under Article 14 and the proportionality standard articulated in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017).

Enforcement actions illustrate the discretion‑accountability tension. In 2022‑23, the ED attached assets worth ₹1,200 crore in the “CoinSwitch Kuber” investigation, invoking Section 5 of the PMLA. The Delhi High Court, in WazirX v. Union of India (2023), upheld the ED’s provisional attachment but directed that the exchange be given an opportunity to demonstrate legitimate source of funds. For decision‑making questions, aspirants should focus on: (a) the distinction between tax treatment (Income‑Tax Act) and regulatory treatment (pending Crypto Bill); (b) the role of FIU‑IND in AML compliance; (c) the RBI’s residual powers over banking access; and (d) the judicial requirement that any restriction be proportionate and non‑arbitrary.

Decision‑Making in the Allocation of 5G Spectrum and the Role of the Telecom Regulatory Authority

The Department of Telecommunications (DoT) conducted the 5G spectrum auction in July‑August 2022, offering 72 GHz across low‑band (600 MHz, 700 MHz), mid‑band (3.3‑3.67 GHz), and high‑band (26 GHz) frequencies. The auction design followed the Simultaneous Multiple Round Ascending (SMRA) format recommended by the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) in its 2021 “Recommendations on Auction of Spectrum in 5G Bands”. TRAI’s discretion encompassed reserve price determination, block size, spectrum cap (50 % per band per licensee), and the introduction of a “spectrum sharing” and “spectrum trading” framework under the Unified License (UL) conditions. The reserve price for the 3.3‑3.67 GHz band was set at ₹317 crore per MHz, a figure derived from the 2021 valuation methodology that incorporated international benchmarks, opportunity cost, and the “willingness‑to‑pay” model.

The auction resulted in total bids of ₹1.5 lakh crore, with Reliance Jio, Bharti Airtel, and Vodafone Idea acquiring the bulk of mid‑band spectrum. Post‑auction, the DoT exercised discretion in granting the “Spectrum Assignment Letter” and in approving the “Spectrum Sharing Agreement” between Jio and Airtel for the 800 MHz band, a first under the 2021 sharing guidelines. The Wireless Planning and Coordination Wing (WPC) monitors compliance with rollout obligations: each licensee must achieve 5G coverage in at least 50 % of the licensed service area within three years and 90 % within five years, failing which the DoT may invoke the “Spectrum Re‑farming” clause.

Judicial review has been limited but instructive. In Cellular Operators Association of India v. Union of India (2023), the Delhi High Court upheld TRAI’s reserve‑price methodology, noting that the authority’s expert discretion in economic valuation is entitled to deference unless shown to be arbitrary. The Supreme Court, in a 2024 special leave petition, declined to interfere with the spectrum cap, reiterating that policy choices on market structure fall within the executive’s domain. However, the Court emphasised that the DoT must publish reasoned orders when invoking penalties for rollout defaults, aligning with the duty to give reasons under Article 14.

For situational‑judgment questions, the decision nodes are: (i) TRAI’s recommendation‑making power versus DoT’s final auction design authority; (ii) the interplay between spectrum sharing/trading rules and the UL conditions; (iii) the rollout obligation timeline and the consequences of non‑compliance; (iv) the standard of judicial review — Wednesbury unreasonableness versus structured proportionality — applied to reserve‑price and cap decisions. Aspirants should be able to trace a scenario (e.g., a new entrant challenging the reserve price) through the administrative hierarchy: TRAI recommendation → DoT acceptance → auction → assignment → rollout monitoring → penalty → judicial review.

Administrative Discretion in Inter‑State Water Dispute Resolution: The Role of the Central Water Commission and Tribunal Awards

The Inter‑State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 (ISRWD Act) provides the statutory architecture for adjudicating disputes between riparian states. Under Section 4, the Central Government may constitute a Water Disputes Tribunal whose award, once published in the Official Gazette, becomes binding on the parties (Section 6). The Central Water Commission (CWC), an attached office of the Ministry of Jal Shakti, performs the technical appraisal: it prepares the “Water Availability Study”, the “Hydrological Data Compendium”, and the “Project Feasibility Reports” that form the evidentiary base for the Tribunal. The CWC’s discretion lies in selecting the hydrological model (e.g., SWAT, MIKE BASIN), defining the baseline period (typically 30 years), and deciding the allocation methodology — whether “equitable apportionment”, “priority of use”, or “historical utilisation”.

Landmark tribunals illustrate the discretion‑outcome link. The Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal (constituted 1990, final award 2007, modified by Supreme Court 2018) adopted a “monthly release schedule” based on the 1924 agreement and the 1976 interim order, but the CWC’s 2005 “Cauvery Basin Study” introduced a 10‑year moving average for inflow estimation, which the Tribunal accepted.
